prayer.text: Saint John Chrysostom, pray for us.

cues.text: From the Law Courts to the Desert
Born around 347 in Antioch , one of the great cities of the ancient Christian East, John trained first as an orator and lawyer under the celebrated pagan teacher Libanius.
He turned decisively toward the ascetic life, studying under the bishop Meletius.
He eventually withdrew to the mountains outside the city to live for several years among hermit monks in conditions of severe self-denial.
This extreme asceticism permanently damaged his health, forcing his eventual return to the city.
But it left him, for the rest of his life, with an unshakeable personal authority to speak about wealth, luxury, and self-denial.
He had, quite literally, given his own body over to the pursuit of holiness before he ever asked his congregations to give anything at all.
The Golden Mouth of Antioch
Ordained priest in 386, John spent the following twelve years preaching almost continuously in Antioch.

He delivered an extraordinary series of biblical homilies — verse-by-verse expositions of entire books of Scripture — that remain, to this day, among the richest treasuries of patristic biblical commentary the Church possesses.

His eloquence was so extraordinary, and so evidently placed at the service of ordinary believers rather than academic display, that within his own lifetime he had already earned the surname by which history would remember him: Chrysostom , "Golden-Mouthed."
He was a preacher, we might say, whose gift was not merely to speak beautifully but to make the plainest truths of the Gospel land, unmistakably, in the conscience of every listener.
A Reluctant Patriarch
In 397, against his own wishes, John was virtually kidnapped by imperial agents and taken to Constantinople to be consecrated Patriarch of the imperial capital.
It was a see whose clergy had grown accustomed to considerable comfort and whose court was thick with the very kind of luxury and intrigue John's Antiochene preaching had always condemned.
John set at once about genuine reform.
He reduced the lavish expenses of the episcopal household and redirected the funds saved to found hospitals for the poor and the sick.
He insisted that the clergy under his authority live with a seriousness matching their office.
These reforms won him the fierce devotion of ordinary Christians and the equally fierce enmity of the wealthy and powerful whose comfortable habits he had disturbed.
The Price of Plain Speech
John's outspoken denunciations of extravagance eventually reached, unmistakably, the imperial court itself.

The Empress Eudoxia , who took his preaching as a personal affront, joined forces with a rival churchman, Theophilus of Alexandria, to engineer John's condemnation and exile at a hastily assembled synod in 403.
A sudden earthquake that same night, widely read by the frightened populace as a sign of divine displeasure, forced his brief recall.
But the peace was short-lived.
In 404 John was exiled a second and final time, this time far into the remote frontier regions of the empire.
A fire that broke out in Constantinople immediately after his departure was blamed, almost certainly unjustly, on his grieving supporters.
Death on the Road

John appealed his case directly to Pope Innocent I in Rome, who recognized the injustice of his condemnation and refused to acknowledge his removal, but imperial power in the East proved unmoved by Roman protest.
Forced on a brutal midsummer march toward an even more remote place of banishment, his already fragile health finally gave out at Comana in Pontus on September 14, 407.
His last recorded words, offered not in bitterness but in praise, were simply: Glory to God for all things .
Legacy
In 438, more than three decades after his death, John's relics were solemnly returned to Constantinople and received with public honor by an emperor.
That emperor was himself the son of the very Eudoxia who had exiled him.
It was a quiet, belated vindication history rarely grants so completely.
To this day, the Divine Liturgy celebrated on most Sundays throughout the Eastern Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Churches still bears his name, the Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom.
His voice, once silenced by imperial power, still shapes the worship of hundreds of millions of Christians every single week.
